guide.summary: Unit 2 covers how atoms bond and how bond type and molecular shape determine properties. You need to classify bonds, read potential energy curves, explain properties of ionic solids, metals, and alloys, draw Lewis diagrams with formal charge and resonance, and predict geometry, polarity, and hybridization with VSEPR.

sections.heading: Bond types and potential energy
sections.body: Electronegativity difference sorts bonds: nonpolar covalent (≈0), polar covalent, and ionic (large difference, typically metal + nonmetal). A potential energy vs. internuclear distance curve has a minimum: the distance at the minimum is the bond length and the depth of the well is the bond energy. Higher bond order means shorter, stronger bonds; larger atoms give longer, usually weaker bonds.

sections.heading: Ionic solids, metals, and alloys
sections.body: Ionic solids are lattices of cations and anions held by Coulombic attraction: high melting points, brittle (a shifted layer puts like charges next to each other), and conductive only when molten or dissolved. Metals are cations in a sea of delocalized electrons: conductive, malleable, ductile. Substitutional alloys (brass: Zn replaces Cu) form from atoms of similar size. Interstitial alloys (steel: C in Fe) put small atoms in the gaps, which makes the metal harder and less malleable because layers can't slide as easily.

sections.heading: Lewis diagrams, formal charge, and resonance
sections.body: Count valence electrons, connect atoms with single bonds, complete octets on outer atoms, then form multiple bonds if the central atom lacks an octet. Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons). The best structure minimizes formal charges and places negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. Resonance means the real structure is an average: in NO₃⁻, all three N–O bonds are identical with bond order 4/3. Elements in period 3 and beyond can exceed an octet (SF₆, XeF₄).

sections.heading: VSEPR, polarity, and hybridization
sections.body: Electron domains (bonds of any order and lone pairs) repel. 2 domains: linear 180°, sp. 3: trigonal planar 120°, sp². 4: tetrahedral 109.5°, sp³. 5: trigonal bipyramidal. 6: octahedral. Lone pairs compress bond angles: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ ≈ 107° > H₂O ≈ 104.5°. Molecular shapes with lone pairs include bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar. A molecule is polar if bond dipoles don't cancel. Each single bond is one σ bond; a double bond is 1σ + 1π; a triple bond is 1σ + 2π.

sections.heading: Worked example: Lewis structure and shape
sections.body: For SO₂, count valence electrons: 6 (S) + 2 × 6 (O) = 18. Place S in the center, form single bonds to each O (4 electrons), complete octets on the O atoms (12 electrons), and place the remaining 2 electrons on S as a lone pair. S now has only 6 electrons, so convert one O lone pair into a double bond, giving resonance structures with one double and one single bond. With two bonding domains and one lone pair, the electron-domain geometry is trigonal planar and the molecular shape is bent, with a bond angle slightly less than 120°. The molecule is polar because its bond dipoles do not cancel.

sections.heading: Worked example: formal charge
sections.body: Formal charge = valence electrons − (nonbonding electrons + ½ bonding electrons). In the structure O=C=O, each O has 6 − (4 + 2) = 0 and C has 4 − (0 + 4) = 0, so the structure has all zero formal charges and is preferred. When several structures are possible, choose the one with formal charges closest to zero and any negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom.

sections.heading: Explaining properties
sections.body: Ionic solids have high melting points because strong Coulombic attractions hold ions in a lattice; compounds with smaller, more highly charged ions (such as MgO compared with NaCl) have stronger attractions and higher melting points. Metals conduct electricity because of delocalized electrons. Interstitial alloys, like steel, contain small atoms in the gaps of a metal lattice and are harder and less malleable, while substitutional alloys, like brass, replace some atoms with others of similar size.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding, bond length and energy, lattice energy, alloy, Lewis structure, resonance, formal charge, VSEPR, hybridization, polarity, and sigma and pi bonds.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students often forget to count all valence electrons or place lone pairs incorrectly.

keyTakeaways: PE curve: minimum position = bond length, well depth = bond energy.
Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond.
Ionic solids are brittle; metals are malleable due to delocalized electrons.
Interstitial alloys are harder and less malleable than the pure metal.
Best Lewis structure: minimal formal charges, negative on the most electronegative atom.
Lone pairs shrink bond angles and often create polarity.
commonMistakes: Treating resonance structures as switching back and forth rather than as one averaged structure.
Counting only bonding pairs (not lone pairs) when determining electron geometry.
Calling a molecule nonpolar just because it has polar bonds that 'look' balanced, without checking lone pairs.
Saying ionic solids conduct electricity as solids.
Forgetting that a multiple bond counts as one electron domain.
examTips: Expect Lewis structure and geometry parts in FRQs; describe the structure clearly (atoms, bonds, lone pairs).
PE-curve questions compare two bonds; reason from atomic size and bond order.
Properties questions want a particle-level reason: delocalized electrons, ion layers, interstitial atoms.
Count σ and π bonds carefully in organic molecules, including C–H bonds.
guide.cramSheet:
**Bonds:** ΔEN small → nonpolar · medium → polar · large → ionic

**PE curve:** min = length · depth = energy · higher order = shorter, stronger

**Solids:** ionic brittle, high mp · metals malleable, conductive · interstitial alloy harder

**Formal charge:** V − N − B/2 · minimize · negative on most EN

**VSEPR:** 2 lin sp · 3 trig planar sp² · 4 tetra sp³ · 5 TBP · 6 oct · lone pairs shrink angles

**σ/π:** single 1σ · double 1σ1π · triple 1σ2π

vocab.definition: The number of shared electron pairs between two atoms, averaged over resonance structures.
The energy required to break one mole of a given bond in the gas phase.
Valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½ bonding electrons; used to choose the best Lewis structure.
Representation of a structure that cannot be described by one Lewis diagram; the real structure is an average.
A region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair or a bond of any order.
Mixing of atomic orbitals to form new orbitals that match the electron-domain geometry (sp, sp², sp³).
A bond formed by head-on orbital overlap; every single bond is a σ bond.
A bond formed by side-by-side overlap of p orbitals; present in double and triple bonds.
An alloy in which small atoms fill spaces between larger metal atoms (e.g., steel).
An alloy in which atoms of similar size replace host atoms in the lattice (e.g., brass).
Electrons free to move throughout a metallic lattice, giving conductivity and malleability.
A net dipole resulting when bond dipoles do not cancel due to geometry.

practice.stem: What is the molecular geometry of NH₃?
practice.explanation: N has 4 electron domains (3 bonds, 1 lone pair): tetrahedral electron geometry, trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

practice.stem: Steel is made by adding a small amount of carbon to iron. Steel is best classified as
practice.explanation: Carbon atoms are much smaller than iron atoms and occupy the spaces between them.

practice.stem: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in CO₂?
practice.explanation: C has two electron domains (two double bonds): linear, sp.

distractors.B: Counts bonds as 4 domains or misreads double bonds.

practice.explanation: NH₃'s lone pair makes it trigonal pyramidal, so the N–H dipoles don't cancel. The others are symmetric.

practice.stem: Potential energy curves are plotted for Cl₂ and Br₂. Compared with the Cl₂ curve, the Br₂ curve has its minimum

choices.text: at a shorter distance and lower (deeper) energy
at the same distance, because both bonds are single bonds
at a longer distance and deeper, because Br has more electrons
at a longer distance and less deep, because Br atoms are larger and the bond is weaker

practice.explanation: Br's valence orbitals are larger (n = 4), giving a longer bond with weaker attraction between nuclei and shared electrons.

distractors.B: Bond order is equal, but atomic size differs.

practice.stem: Which Lewis structure for the cyanate ion, OCN⁻, is the most important contributor?

choices.text: N≡C–O with three lone pairs on O (formal charge −1 on O)
N=C=O with two lone pairs on each end (formal charge −1 on N)
N–C≡O with three lone pairs on N (formal charges −2 on N, +1 on O)
C in the center bonded to nothing, with ions O⁻ and N

practice.explanation: A and B both have one −1 formal charge, but A places it on O, the more electronegative atom. C has larger formal charges.

distractors.B: Valid but minor: negative charge on the less electronegative N.

practice.stem: Which ranks H–X–H bond angles from largest to smallest, with the correct reason?

choices.text: H₂O > NH₃ > CH₄, because O is most electronegative
All are equal at 109.5°, because all have four electron domains
CH₄ > NH₃ > H₂O, because lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs
NH₃ > CH₄ > H₂O, because N has one lone pair

practice.explanation: Each has four domains, but lone pairs occupy more space; more lone pairs compress angles more: 109.5°, ≈107°, ≈104.5°.

practice.stem: Experiments show all three N–O bonds in NO₃⁻ have the same length. This is best explained by

choices.text: the ion rapidly switching between three structures with one double bond each
resonance: electrons are delocalized, so each N–O bond has a bond order of 4/3
all three bonds being double bonds
all three bonds being single bonds with N having an expanded octet

practice.explanation: The real structure is an average of the resonance forms: 4 bonding pairs spread over 3 bonds.

distractors.A: Common misconception; resonance is not oscillation.

practice.stem: Why does solid NaCl shatter when struck, while solid copper bends?

choices.text: Copper has a higher melting point than NaCl.
NaCl's covalent bonds are weaker than copper's metallic bonds.
Shifting a layer of NaCl brings like-charged ions next to each other, causing repulsion; in Cu, delocalized electrons keep cations bonded as layers slide.
NaCl molecules are polar and copper atoms are nonpolar.

practice.explanation: Brittleness of ionic solids and malleability of metals both come from how the lattice responds to displacement.

distractors.D: NaCl is not made of molecules.
distractors.A: True (Cu melts at a higher temperature), but melting point doesn't explain brittleness vs. malleability.

practice.stem: How many valence electrons are in the Lewis structure of the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻?
practice.explanation: S 6 + 3 × O 6 = 24, plus 2 for the 2− charge = 26.

practice.stem: Which molecule has lone pairs on its central atom but is nonpolar?
practice.explanation: XeF₄ has 6 domains (4 bonds, 2 lone pairs opposite each other): square planar, so the Xe–F dipoles cancel.

practice.stem: Acrylonitrile is H₂C=CH–C≡N. How many σ and π bonds does it contain?

distractors.B: Misses one C–H or the C–C bond.

practice.stem: Which explanation best accounts for steel being harder and less malleable than pure iron?

choices.text: Carbon replaces iron atoms, forming ionic bonds that make the lattice brittle.
Carbon atoms in the spaces between iron atoms disrupt the regular lattice and make it harder for layers of iron atoms to slide past each other.
Carbon removes the delocalized electrons from iron.
Carbon atoms are larger than iron atoms and push layers apart.

practice.explanation: In an interstitial alloy, small atoms in the interstices pin the layers, increasing rigidity.

distractors.A: Steel is interstitial, not substitutional or ionic.

practice.stem: Rank the carbon–oxygen bond length in CO, CO₂, and CO₃²⁻ from shortest to longest.

choices.text: All equal, because all are C–O bonds

practice.explanation: Bond orders: CO 3, CO₂ 2, CO₃²⁻ 4/3 (resonance). Higher bond order means a shorter bond.

practice.prompt: Formaldehyde, CH₂O, and methanol, CH₃OH, both contain carbon–oxygen bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe a complete Lewis electron-dot diagram for CH₂O, showing all bonds and lone pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the approximate H–C–H bond angle in CH₂O and the hybridization of the carbon atom.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify which molecule has the shorter carbon–oxygen bond. Justify your answer in terms of bond order.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The O atom in CH₃OH has two lone pairs. Identify the approximate C–O–H bond angle, and explain why it is less than 109.5°.

rubric.description: C central with single bonds to two H, a double bond to O, and two lone pairs on O (12 valence electrons).
CH₂O, because its C–O bond is a double bond (order 2) versus a single bond (order 1) in CH₃OH; more shared electrons pull nuclei closer.
About 104–109° (accept 'about 105°'); the two lone pairs on O repel the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs do, compressing the angle.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Carbon is central. It forms single bonds to each of two H atoms and a double bond to O. O carries two lone pairs. Total 12 valence electrons (C 4 + 2 H 2 + O 6).

(b) Carbon has three electron domains (trigonal planar), so the H–C–H angle is about 120°, and carbon is sp² hybridized.

(c) CH₂O has the shorter C–O bond. Its C–O bond is a double bond (bond order 2), while CH₃OH has a single C–O bond (bond order 1). More shared electron pairs increase attraction between the nuclei and bonding electrons, pulling the atoms closer.

(d) About 105°. O has four electron domains, but two are lone pairs. Lone pairs occupy more space and repel bonding pairs more strongly, compressing the C–O–H angle below the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°.
